Neonates of the opossum shrimp Neomysis integer emerge from the brood pouch at a total length of 0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm], a diminutive size typical of mysid juveniles. This initial length corresponds to a remarkably low dry weight at birth of approximately 0.0000295 g , reflecting the limited yolk reserves invested per offspring. Growth proceeds through a series of moults, and the length at metamorphosis, identified as the inflection point in length-at-age curves, is recorded at 0.5 cm . This morphological transformation marks the transition from the planktonic larval phase to a more benthic post-metamorphic juvenile lifestyle. Juveniles then continue a phase of rapid somatic expansion, during which the allometric shifts in body proportions become evident as they approach the length at puberty.

Reproductive maturation in Neomysis integer follows a well-defined schedule that is strongly modulated by ambient temperature. At a constant temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the time since birth at puberty is reported to be 110 days [tp = 110 days], a duration that encompasses approximately 15 to 16 successive moulting events. In stark contrast, when individuals are reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], this developmental phase is compressed considerably, with the interval from birth to the pubertal moult reduced to 45 days [tp = 45 days]. This marked acceleration underscores the profound influence of thermal regime on crustacean ontogeny, as higher temperatures drive faster metabolic and growth rates. The attainment of functional sexual maturity, signaled by the first appearance of ovigerous females in the population, is therefore much earlier under warmer conditions.

Embryonic development within the marsupium also shows a pronounced dependence on temperature. At 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from oviposition to the release of free-swimming larvae, is approximately 37 days [ab = approximately 37 days]. When the temperature is raised to 15 °C [T = 15 °C], this incubation period is nearly halved, resulting in an age at birth of 19 days [ab = 19 days]. The overall life span of Neomysis integer is also constrained by thermal conditions; at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum recorded longevity reaches about 365 days [am = about 365 days], after which senescence and natural mortality typically intervene. These life-history metrics illustrate a classic temperature-driven trade-off between developmental rate and total lifespan.

Adult body size in Neomysis integer reaches a well-defined asymptote, with the ultimate length recorded at 1.7 cm [Li = 1.7 cm], a value typical of this coastal mysid species. This maximum total length is associated with a corresponding ultimate dry weight of approximately 0.0105 g , a measure derived from length-weight relationships established for related mysids. The length at puberty, which is the size threshold at which reproductive structures become functional, is 0.8 cm [Lp = 0.8 cm]. At this pubertal stage, the dry weight of the animal is approximately 0.0011 g , representing a notable increase from the negligible mass at birth. The shift from the juvenile growth phase to the reproductive adult phase thus occurs at a body size that is roughly half of the ultimate length.

The population dynamics of Neomysis integer are tightly coupled to these thermal and ontogenetic parameters. At 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the interval from birth to the pubertal moult is 45 days [tp = 45 days], whereas at the cooler 10 °C [T = 10 °C] this same developmental milestone requires 110 days [tp = 110 days], resulting in a shorter generation time and potentially higher population turnover in warmer estuaries. The limited lifespan of approximately one year at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] further constrains the number of reproductive bouts an individual can achieve, with a maximum recorded longevity of about 365 days [am = about 365 days]. The diminutive size at birth (0.2 cm [Lb = 0.2 cm]) and corresponding dry mass (0.0000295 g ) make early life stages highly susceptible to predation, a vulnerability compounded by the thermal sensitivity of developmental rates when temperatures fall below 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. These integrated life-history traits ultimately define the ecological role of N. integer as a key prey item in coastal food webs.
